title: Effect of beta-Blocker Withdrawal on Functional Capacity in Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction
authors: Palau P, Seller J, Dominguez E, Sastre C, Ramon JM, de La Espriella R, et al.
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
followUp: two 2-week treatment periods separated by a 2-week washout
population: Patients with stable heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, New York Heart Association class II or III, chronotropic incompetence and previous beta-blocker treatment, in a multicentre trial sponsored from Valencia, Spain; mean age 72.6 years, 59.6% women
funder: Supported by grants from the Spanish Ministry of Economy and Competitiveness through the Carlos III Health Institute (Fondos de Investigacion Sanitaria PI17/01426), co-funded with European Regional Development Fund and Centro de Investigacion Biomedica en Red Enfermedades Cardiovascular funds (16/11/00420 and 16/11/00403); the authors report no relationships relevant to the paper. Registry NCT03871803 names the Fundacion para la Investigacion del Hospital Clinico de Valencia as sponsor. A post hoc report of the same trial states that the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis or publication.
result: Multicentre, randomised, investigator-blinded crossover trial of withdrawing (n = 26) against continuing (n = 26) beta-blocker treatment, then the opposite. Peak oxygen consumption rose after withdrawal, 14.3 against 12.2 ml/kg/min (difference +2.1, P < 0.001), and percentage of predicted peak oxygen consumption 81.1% against 69.4% (+11.7%, P < 0.001). Heart rate at peak exercise was higher after withdrawal (least-square means 127 against 97 beats per minute, P < 0.001), and the change in peak oxygen consumption correlated positively with the change in peak heart rate.
